events.desc: There is, of course, absolutely nothing under the kitchen floor. And watching three grown men dig for it with such earnest conviction — well. Some pleasures are simply too exquisite to rush.
events.thinking:
**Tommy presses his ear to the flagstone and my face is splitting.** The grin pushes up from behind my breastbone and there is nothing I can do about it — nothing I want to do about it. My jaw loosens completely, the muscles giving way like something unpinning, a release that starts in my face and spreads downward through my throat and into my chest where it sits heavy and warm and widening. Danny's brow furrows. He shifts the butter knife to a new seam with such careful attention that my breathing deepens around the watching — each second of his concentration is a second I am inside, holding, the gap between what they believe and what I know opening into something that fills my whole chest. There is no silver. There never was. The knowing sits behind my sternum like something held on the tongue, turned slowly, the warmth sharpening with each earnest scrape of metal on stone. At ten I watched through the schoolyard window while the older boy dug and dug and dug — the same warmth, the same widening, the same body wanting to stay inside the moment forever. My body remembers the window ledge under my forearms, the glass cool against my face.

**Sparks raps a flagstone and pauses — listens — raps again.** The sincerity of it arrives in my sternum like a second helping. My jaw has loosened past the point of Foxworth's polished composure and I don't care — the grin is wider than any face I've built and it is pushing outward through my chest, my shoulders, my arms, reaching into my fingers. Time has stretched. Each second holds more weight than it should. Tommy shifts to a second flagstone and the warmth deepens — not the gut's hollow hunger, not the fingertips' lateral fizzing, but the breastbone's own slow heat, the one that lives only in the distance between what they are doing and what is true. Danny wipes sweat from his forehead. My breathing is deep and even and unhurried.

**My peripheral attention pulls toward the corridor.** The library path is clear — my fingertips read the angle without my gaze leaving Danny's knees on the stone. At this pace, twelve minutes before they tire. If Danny gives up first, eight. The geometry maps itself through my hands — corridor, staircase, library door — each distance fizzing into sequence, the lateral current running through my fingers alongside the breastbone warmth but utterly different from it. The warmth wants stillness. The fizzing wants movement. Both are here. My weight shifts half an inch toward the corridor, the body already preparing for the transition it hasn't decided on.

**Danny pauses.** He frowns. He taps the same flagstone again, harder, with more hope. The warmth spreads into my shoulders, my arms, my fingers. I want this to last. I want every second of their sincere, futile digging to stretch further, to hold longer, to sit heavier in my chest. The grin catches me again and I let it. My sternum is full. The corridor is patient. Everything is exactly where I put it.
